outcome: Since 26 January 2024 Linnik's constant L (the exponent in the least-prime bound, the quantity the linked article names) has been claimed moved to 3.99 (Naslund, GitHub and Hexagon, 1-2 October 2026; authors state AI systems wrote the paper; no human review found) and to 7/3 and 12/5 (teal-sea pull request #277, 8 October 2026; agent-written, conditional on OpenAI's unrefereed 7/8 zero-free-region manuscript and Chen-Gupta-Li's density estimate); the best unconditional value in the sources read is still 5 (Xylouris, 2011); conditional results (GLH, GRH plus a pair-correlation hypothesis) and a Linnik-Goldbach update (GRH: 6 powers of two) also appeared in the window.
problem_asks: The bullet names no problem. Its statement is 'Problems associated to Linnik's theorem' and it links the article Linnik's theorem, so the record takes as the reading the open problems that the linked article itself lists (Part A-B-C below). Part A: Linnik's constant L, the least exponent such that for every modulus d and every a coprime to d the least prime p(a,d) in the progression a mod d satisfies p(a,d) << d^L. Linnik's theorem that some such L exists (1944) is known; what is open is the value of the optimal L (the infimum of admissible exponents). Part B: the conjectured bound p(a,d) < d^2 for all d (the article writes 'It is also conjectured that'; it cites Heath-Brown 1992; literature sources credit Kanold and Schinzel-Sierpinski for this form). Part C (not in the article's own wording; named in literature searched): Heath-Brown's conjecture p(d) << d (log d)^2 with the least prime taken over all residue classes. Part D (listed in the article, conditional, not open as stated): under GRH, p(a,d) << phi(d)^2 (log d)^2 (article cites Lamzouri, Li, Soundararajan 2015). Alternative reading (not named by the linked article; recorded so the judging pass can decide): the Linnik-Goldbach problem, Part E: the least K such that every sufficiently large even integer is a sum of two primes and K powers of 2 (Linnik's theorem on Goldbach numbers). Parts A-D are the reading the linked article supports; E is a second reading the record covers separately.

events.what_happened: D. R. Heath-Brown, 'Zero-free regions for Dirichlet L-functions, and the least prime in an arithmetic progression', Proc. London Math. Soc. 64 (1992) 265-338. Gives an unconditional bound p(a,d) << d^5.5 (exponent 5.5, as cited by later papers and by the Wikipedia Bounds table) and, under GRH, p(a,d) << (phi(d) log d)^2. Known here only from citing sources and the Wikipedia article; the paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Part A: unconditional admissible exponent 5.5 (an upper bound on L). Part D: the GRH-conditional bound (phi(d) log d)^2 as cited. Nothing unconditional toward Part B.
events.remains: Part A below 5.5; Part B; Part C.

checked_by.who: Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (journal of record)

events.direction: Upper bound on Linnik's constant; no lower bound; not an object.

events.what_happened: T. Xylouris, PhD thesis (Bonn), building on Heath-Brown's method, obtains L = 5 (a Bonn seminar abstract of April 2011 gives 'L=5.0'). Later sources give Xylouris's 5.18 or 5.2 for an earlier stage (2009), and a 2018 German write-up, 'Linniks Konstante ist kleiner als 5' (Chebyshevskii Sbornik), records L = 5 with the Wikipedia table listing 'Xylouris 2018: 5 - epsilon'. Sources read only through search snippets and the Wikipedia table; not opened.
events.revisions: Wikipedia table lists L = 5 (2011) and 5 - epsilon (2018); a 2009 figure of 5.18 appears in several secondary sources.
events.delivers: Part A: unconditional admissible exponent 5 (the best unconditional value in every 2024-2026 source read). Part A's 5 - epsilon (2018 write-up) is the sole later refinement the Wikipedia table records before 2026.
events.remains: Part A below 5; Part B; Part C.

checked_by.who: Chebyshevskii Sbornik (2018 write-up, German, Russian and English abstract)
checked_by.what_they_did: published the write-up 'Linniks Konstante ist kleiner als 5'

events.doubts: Sources disagree on the exponent of the first announcement (5.18 in 2009; 5.2 in a 2015 seminar abstract; 5 in 2011). Zhao's 2025 paper attributes 5.2 to Xylouris (2009) (see the disputes entry). The thesis itself was not read.
events.direction: Upper bound on L; not an object.

events.what_happened: Under GRH the least prime satisfies p(a,d) <= phi(d)^2 (log d)^2. The Wikipedia Linnik article cites Lamzouri, Li and Soundararajan (2015), 'Conditional bounds for the least quadratic non-residue and related problems', and says the bound 'has been also proved'. The paper was not opened; the article's wording may overstate the status (the title says 'conditional').
events.delivers: Part D only: a conditional (GRH) bound. No unconditional content.
events.remains: Parts A, B, C (unconditional).
events.doubts: The journal of record and any refereeing were not established in the sources read; the article's statement 'has been also proved' is taken as cited.
events.direction: Conditional upper bound; not an object.

events.what_happened: J. Thorner and A. Zaman, 'Refinements to the prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions', arXiv:2108.10878 (submitted August 2021, month from arXiv identifier). Proves a uniform prime number theorem in progressions that yields, as corollaries, Siegel-Walfisz, Brun-Titchmarsh, Hoheisel-type results and Linnik's bound on the least prime. Search summaries give no new exponent. Published in Mathematische Zeitschrift 306(3) (2024) per the Illinois repository record. Not opened.
events.revisions: Journal version Math. Z. 306 (3), 2024, article 54, per the Illinois repository record.
events.delivers: Re-proves Linnik's theorem (existence of L) as a corollary; no new value for Part A.
events.remains: Parts A, B, C, D as before.

checked_by.what_they_did: published the paper (March 2024 issue per the repository record)

events.direction: Confirms existence of L by a uniform method; no movement of its value.

events.what_happened: J. B. Friedlander and H. Iwaniec, 'Selberg's sieve of irregular density', arXiv:2206.03479 (submitted 7 June 2022; Acta Arithmetica 209 (2023) 385-396), gives a sieve-based proof of Linnik's theorem in the presence of exceptional zeros; companion 'Sifting for small primes from an arithmetic progression', arXiv:2303.06122 (March 2023; Science China Mathematics 66 (2023) 2715-2730), completes a sieve proof that avoids log-free zero-density bounds and zero repulsion. Search summaries do not state a record exponent; one secondary summary gives L = 75,744,000 for the sieve argument, which was not checked. Neither paper was opened.
events.revisions: Acta Arithmetica 209 (2023) and Science China Mathematics 66 (2023) for the companion.
events.delivers: A new, L-function-free-in-part proof of Linnik's theorem (existence of L) with no record exponent stated in the sources read.
events.remains: Part A's value; Parts B, C, D.

checked_by.who: Acta Arithmetica and Science China Mathematics (journals of record)

events.doubts: The 75,744,000 figure appears only in a secondary summary and was not checked against the paper.
events.direction: Alternative proof method for Linnik's theorem; no movement in the value of L stated.

events.what_happened: D. R. Heath-Brown and J.-C. Puchta, 'Integers represented as a sum of primes and powers of two', arXiv:math/0201299 (January 2002; New York J. Math. 9 (2003)). Every sufficiently large even integer is a sum of two primes and 13 powers of 2 unconditionally, and 7 under GRH. This is the Part E (Linnik-Goldbach) reading. Not opened; search summaries only.
events.delivers: Part E (Linnik-Goldbach reading only): K <= 13 unconditional; K <= 7 under GRH. Nothing for Parts A-D.
events.remains: Part E below 13 (unconditional) and 7 (GRH).

checked_by.who: New York Journal of Mathematics (journal of record)

events.direction: Upper bounds on the Linnik-Goldbach K; not an object.

events.what_happened: J. Pintz and I. Ruzsa, 'On Linnik's approximation to Goldbach's problem. II', Acta Mathematica Hungarica 161(2) (2020) 569-582: eight powers of 2 suffice unconditionally (K = 8), and seven under GRH. Pintz's 2020 seminar abstract describes the result as 'announced many years ago and worked out recently'. Read through search summaries and Johnston-Trudgian; the paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Part E (Linnik-Goldbach reading only): K <= 8 unconditional; K <= 7 under GRH.
events.remains: Part E: K <= 7 unconditional and below 7 under GRH (later claims are in the window, see johnston-trudgian-2026); Parts A-D untouched.
events.doubts: Pintz's talk describes the work as 'announced many years ago and worked out recently', so the write-up date rather than the announcement is used.
events.direction: Upper bound on the Linnik-Goldbach K; not an object.

events.what_happened: A Springer-hosted paper (DOI 10.1007/s11854-019-0060-4; journal name and authors not read) improves the Linnik exponent for primes in progressions modulo powers of a fixed prime to L < 2.1115, from 12/5 (the abstract snippet prints '2.2' for 12/5, a typo noted by the search summary). It combines Postnikov (1956) and Korobov (1974) double Weyl-sum estimates with Gallagher (1972) and Iwaniec (1974). Year inferred from the DOI; not verified.
events.delivers: A restricted case of Part A: moduli that are powers of one fixed prime. Not the general constant.
events.remains: Part A for all moduli; Parts B, C, D.
events.doubts: Year and journal are inferred from the DOI and were not confirmed. Restricted to prime-power moduli.
events.direction: Upper bound for a restricted class of moduli; not an object.

events.what_happened: K. Matomaki, J. Merikoski and J. Terävainen, 'Primes in arithmetic progressions and short intervals without L-functions', arXiv:2401.17570, v1 submitted 31 January 2024 (only version). A sieve for primes in multiplicatively structured sets gives a new L-function-free proof of Linnik's problem: the least prime p = a mod q satisfies p << q^350 (Theorem 1.1, stated without hypothesis for q large), and a short-interval result for (x - x^{39/40}, x]. The index-2 subgroup case is handled by a treatment the authors attribute to Friedlander and Iwaniec.
events.delivers: Part A: an unconditional admissible exponent 350 by a new method. Weaker than the record 5, so the value of L's infimum is not moved. Parts B, C, D not addressed.
events.remains: Part A below 5 (the record is unchanged in the sources read); Parts B, C.
events.doubts: The exponent 350 is far from the record; the unconditional status of the index-2 case depends on the cited Friedlander-Iwaniec treatment.
events.direction: Confirms Linnik's theorem by a new route with a weak exponent; cuts neither way on the value of L.

events.what_happened: A. Fiori, 'The Least Prime in Arithmetic Progression', arXiv:2404.02329 (v1 2 April 2024). Updates Wagstaff's 1979 computations of the least prime in progressions, refines Wagstaff's conjecture, and conjectures that for n > 3 the least prime bound is 3 phi(n) log(n) log(phi(n)), verified numerically to 10^8. Conjecture and computation; no proof.
events.delivers: A numerically supported conjectured refinement of the least-prime bound at the scale of Part C; no theorem; nothing for Part A.
events.remains: Parts A, B, C (proof), D.
events.directly_checkable: The numerical bound up to 10^8 is checkable by the authors' tables (two large data tables are noted on the page); not rerun.
events.doubts: Conjecture supported only by computation to 10^8.
events.direction: No counterexample reported up to 10^8; no movement of L.

events.what_happened: L. Hu and S. Liu, 'A pair of Goldbach-Linnik equations in unlike powers of primes and powers of two', arXiv:2408.13458 (v1 24 August 2024). Every pair of large even integers satisfying the necessary conditions is a pair of one prime, one prime square, two prime cubes and 56 powers of 2. Keywords and title place it in the Linnik-Goldbach line.
events.delivers: Part E variant only: a pair of equations with mixed prime powers and 56 powers of 2. Not the single-equation Linnik-Goldbach problem.
events.remains: All of Parts A-D; Part E for the single-equation problem.
events.doubts: Different problem (a pair of equations, mixed prime powers).
events.direction: Different problem; cuts nowhere on Part E as stated.

events.what_happened: G. Zhao, 'The exceptional set of Goldbach problem and Linnik's constant', arXiv:2511.05631 (v1 7 November 2025; v2 23 January 2026). Proves a Goldbach exceptional-set bound E(X) = O(X^{7/10}) with ineffective constant. The abstract says 'the method applied here also leads to P(q) = O(q^5)', where P(q) is the least prime in a progression mod q. In the text the author writes that the method 'clearly shows L=5 is admissible', presented as improving on the 5.2 attributed to Xylouris (2009).
events.delivers: Part A: a claim that L = 5 is admissible by a method attributed to Pintz. That value is already the record (Xylouris 2011), so nothing below 5 is established; the 'improvement' from 5.2 is a re-attribution question (see disputes). The Goldbach exceptional-set bound is a different problem (not in scope).
events.remains: Part A below 5; Parts B, C, D; Part E not addressed by this paper.
events.doubts: The text says Theorem 1.3 (the P(q) = O(q^5) result) is 'much simpler than Theorem 1.2' and that its proof is omitted, so the Part A claim is not supported by a written proof in the text read. The claimed 5.2-to-5 step conflicts with the literature, which already records 5 from Xylouris (2011).
events.direction: Claims L = 5 (no value below the existing record of 5).

events.what_happened: B. Chen, V. Gupta and Y. C. Li, 'Large value estimates for Dirichlet polynomials with characters and zero density of Dirichlet L-functions', arXiv:2507.08296 (v1 11 July 2025; v2 27 July 2026, current). Proves the sum over characters mod q of N(sigma,T,chi) << (qT)^{7(1-sigma)/3+eps}, a zero-density exponent 7/3 that improves Huxley's 12/5. Abstract applications: a new bound for the least Goldbach number in progressions modulo a prime, and short-interval results for progressions with prime-power moduli. The abstract states no least-prime-in-progression consequence.
events.delivers: A zero-density input only. No least-prime exponent (Part A) and no statement toward Parts B, C. The Goldbach-number bound concerns a different quantity.
events.remains: Parts A-D.
events.doubts: The teal-sea pull request cites it as Theorem 1.2 for its 7/3 claim (see teal-sea-2026-10-08); the paper itself does not claim a Linnik consequence.
events.direction: Density estimate; no direct movement of L.

events.what_happened: C. Bellotti, T. Trudgian and A. Yang, 'Zero-free regions inspired by work of Heath-Brown', arXiv:2603.21490 (v1 23 March 2026). New explicit zero-free region for the Riemann zeta function (no zeros for t >= 3 and sigma >= 1 - 1/(4.896 log t)), drawing on Heath-Brown's Linnik-constant method. States no least-prime bound.
events.delivers: A zero-free region for zeta; no least-prime exponent (no movement of Part A).
events.remains: Parts A-D.
events.direction: Input-type result; cuts nowhere on Part A.

events.what_happened: M. Bruna, 'A conditional bound for the least prime in an arithmetic progression', arXiv:2603.25612 (v1 26 March 2026; the only version listed). Assuming the generalized Lindelof hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions (GLH), P(a,q) <= q^(2+eps) for q large in terms of eps. The abstract says this nearly matches the GRH-implied classical estimate.
events.delivers: Part A under GLH only: admissible exponent 2 + eps, the scale the conjectures predict; not an unconditional move. Relative to Part B, it gives 2 + eps rather than the exact d^2 form.
events.remains: Part A unconditional; Part B exactly; Part C; Part D is already GRH-conditional.
events.doubts: Conditional on GLH, a hypothesis not established; the 2 + eps exponent does not resolve Part B.
events.direction: Conditional bound at the conjectured scale; cuts toward the conjectured exponent only under GLH.

events.what_happened: N. Kandhil, A. Languasco and P. Moree, 'Beyond the Riemann Hypothesis bounds: a pair-correlation approach to the least prime in arithmetic progression and the smallest quadratic non-residue', arXiv:2607.14515 (v1 16 July 2026; 26 pages). Under GRH and a pair-correlation hypothesis for general characters (Hypothesis 2), Theorem 5 gives p(k) << phi(k) exp(B (log k)^A) with A in (1/2, 1), where p(k) is the largest least prime over residues mod k. Since exp((log k)^A) = k^{o(1)}, this is k^{1+o(1)}. A quadratic-character result (Theorem 3) uses RH and Hypothesis 1.
events.delivers: Part C (and Part B only in its conditional form): a GRH-plus-Hypothesis-2 bound of k^{1+o(1)} for the least prime. Unconditionally nothing new. The hypotheses are stated and not proved.
events.remains: Parts A, B, C unconditionally; the hypotheses are unproved.
events.doubts: The result depends on two unproved hypotheses; Hypothesis 2 has a restricted range of k and T. Its relation to known conjectures is for the judging pass.
events.direction: Conditional improvement at the GRH scale; cuts toward the Heath-Brown-type form only under added hypotheses.

events.what_happened: V. Blomer, F. Brumley and M. Radziwill, 'Joint Linnik problems', arXiv:2603.05609 (5 March 2026, 47 pages). Proves a Michel-Venkatesh conjecture on joinings of distinct 'Linnik problems', meaning equidistribution of Linnik points on spheres and CM points on the modular surface, conditional on a splitting condition holding for all but O((log log X)^(1+o(1))) discriminants up to X.
events.delivers: Nothing for this problem: 'Linnik problem' here is an equidistribution question on spheres, not least primes in progressions. Scope excluded; recorded because the name matches.
events.remains: All of Parts A-E.
events.doubts: Different problem sharing a name.
events.direction: Different problem; cuts nowhere on Parts A-E.

events.what_happened: D. R. Johnston and T. Trudgian, 'An update on the Linnik-Goldbach problem', arXiv:2605.17825 (v1 18 May 2026; v2 22 July 2026). Theorem 1: assuming GRH, every sufficiently large even integer is a sum of two primes and K = 6 powers of 2, improving the GRH value 7 of Heath-Brown-Puchta and Pintz-Ruzsa; the gain comes from new Goldbach-representation bounds due to Lichtman (arXiv:2309.08522, 2023, before the window). The authors say they 'fall just short of obtaining K=7 unconditionally with our setup'. An unconditional K = 7 using the Maynard-Pandey-Radziwill exponent (N^(19/24)) appears in Section 3.3 and is called 'preliminary'; the authors do not list it as a theorem and cite a workshop abstract for it. Romanov's problem refinements are also covered.
events.delivers: Part E (Linnik-Goldbach reading only): GRH K <= 6. The unconditional value stays at K <= 8 (Pintz-Ruzsa) in the theorems listed. Nothing for Parts A-D.
events.remains: Part E unconditional (7 is only preliminary); Parts A-D.
events.doubts: The unconditional K = 7 rests on an unpublished workshop announcement that the authors themselves call preliminary. The Linnik-Goldbach reading is not named by the linked article.
events.direction: Improves a conditional Linnik-Goldbach bound; no counterexample; no movement of Part A.

events.what_happened: K. Matomaki and J. Terävainen, 'Linnik's problem for multiplicative functions', arXiv:2605.27833 (v1 27 May 2026; the only version listed). For real multiplicative h, R(h;q) <= q^(2+eps) for the least n in each reduced class carrying h's sign pattern, unless the sign of h 'pretends' to a real character of order at most two. Corollaries for Liouville and Mobius; for Liouville it improves a Ford-Radziwill result. A July 2025 MPIM Bonn seminar abstract presents the same statement; per the dating rule the write-up date is used.
events.delivers: An analogue of Linnik's problem for multiplicative functions (not the least prime in progressions): unconditional q^(2+eps) apart from a character exception. No value for Part A.
events.remains: Parts A-D unaddressed; the character exception.
events.doubts: Analogue, not the stated problem.
events.direction: Analogue result; cuts nowhere on Part A.

events.what_happened: J. Maynard, M. Pandey and M. Radziwill, 'Exponential sums over primes', arXiv:2608.14777 (v1 14 August 2026). For alpha = a/q + eps with q <= N^(1/2), the sum over n < N of Lambda(n) e(n alpha) is bounded by N^(o(1)) (N/B^(1/2) + N^(19/24)), improving the N^(4/5) term of Vinogradov's 1937 bound. Theorem 1.1 has no hypothesis; GRH appears only in a remark. Used as an input to the Johnston-Trudgian update.
events.delivers: An exponential-sum input for the Linnik-Goldbach problem (Part E). No least-prime result, so Parts A-D not addressed.
events.remains: Parts A-D; Part E beyond this exponent.
events.doubts: Johnston-Trudgian call the result preliminary and cite a workshop abstract; the arXiv text mentions no earlier announcement. A separate search snippet credits the N^(19/24) improvement to Maynard alone.
events.direction: Improves an exponential sum bound; no direction on the problem's parts.

events.what_happened: OpenAI, 'The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis: A Zero-Free Half-Plane Re(s) > 7/8', family 003 of the openai/math release (manuscript dated 30 September 2026; the repository of 722 manuscripts was publicly released on 6 October 2026 per secondary coverage). Claims that Dirichlet L-functions, zeta included, have no zeros with Re(s) > 7/8, and the same for finite-order Hecke L-functions over Q(sqrt(-3)), with principal poles excluded. Companion 'Uniform exclusion of Landau-Siegel zeros' (path dated 1 October 2026). A separate Re(s) > 11/12 write-up is described as human-edited for readability. The repository page and Lean scope note state no Linnik result, Linnik constant or least-prime bound.
events.revisions: Three Hodge-related manuscripts withdrawn 7 October 2026 for an unrelated sign error; 14 other manuscripts revised. Revision status of family 003 not checked.
events.delivers: A zero-free region for L-functions with theta = 7/8. It states no least-prime bound. Any bearing on Part A is only through third-party derivations (teal-sea-2026-10-08 and the Wikipedia 2.4 row).
events.remains: Parts A-D; the result is an input to them, not an answer.

Scientific American reports that not all proofs were certified by Lean, that some other proofs were retracted after outside mistakes were found, and that 'No one, not even OpenAI researchers themselves, has been able to even read through everything yet'. The Lean check covers the formal statement, not the informal match. A third-party re-run reporting acceptance by two kernels could not be verified.

events.what_happened: E. Naslund (GitHub handle 'enaslund'), 'Linnik's constant is at most 3.99', repository enaslund/linniks-constant-3.99 (first commit 1 October 2026, 'Linnik's constant is at most 3.99: paper and Lean formalization'; ten commits through 2 October 2026) and Hexagon preprint hexagon:2610.00018v1 (listed as v1, 2 October 2026). Claims: for every sufficiently large modulus q, every reduced residue class mod q contains a prime below q^3.99, so L <= 3.99 for sufficiently large moduli, uniform in the class, improving Xylouris's 5. The analytic argument is conditional on published estimates stated as hypotheses. A Lean 4 / Mathlib (v4.35.0-rc3) formalization covers parts of the argument (18 theorems, including a weighted Heath-Brown near-density estimate and a certificate checker); the bound itself is not proved in Lean. The Palomar registry entry is PALOMAR-2026-10-01-000020 per the repository (the Wikipedia citation gives 000018; the entry page was not readable).
events.revisions: Repository commits 1-2 October 2026; later commits change only the paper and documentation; the Lean files and comparator.json match registered commit ecdbe3e per the repository.
events.delivers: Part A: a claimed admissible exponent 3.99 for sufficiently large moduli, conditional on the listed analytic inputs. If correct it moves the value of L below the record 5. It does not reach Part B (d^2 for all d), Part C, or Part D's conditional content.
events.remains: Part A below 3.99 and the conjectured 2; Part B for all d; Part C; the restriction to sufficiently large moduli.

checked_by.who: Palomar registry review (automated; per repository commit messages 'Address Palomar's review')
checked_by.qualification: registry checks that the Lean compiles and that the formal statement matches the informal one; secondary sources say it performs no human peer review

checked_by.who: AI agents (named as such in the repository)
checked_by.what_they_did: reviewed the formal statements against the printed sources; the README says 'All reviews so far are by AI agents.'

events.directly_checkable: The repository says the proof's computer certificates (commit messages cite 29,397,336 certified linear relaxations) are checked by three separate programs, one formally verified, according to the Hexagon page. Not run here.
events.doubts: (1) The README states: 'No human has yet reviewed the formal statements or refereed the underlying mathematics.' (2) The text is AI-written per the authors (see ai). (3) The case tree, zero-location arguments, family bounds and exterior regimes have only conventional proofs and computer checks, not Lean. (4) The introduction speaks of 'four published estimates' but the Hypotheses table lists six literature inputs plus one derived statement. (5) The Wikipedia Linnik article's history shows a 7 October 2026 edit by the account 'Enaslund' adding new bounds, including the 3.99 row; this is a self-citation in a secondary source, not uptake. (6) No expert commentary was found in any search. (7) The Palomar entry ID differs between the repository and Wikipedia; the registry text was not read.
events.direction: Upper bound L <= 3.99 for sufficiently large moduli, below the record 5; cuts toward the conjectured small L without reaching 2.

events.what_happened: teal-sea (organisation-style handle, no named human), pull request #277 in teal-sea/zeta-lab, 'Hunt #123: Linnik's constant L <= 7/3 given the 7/8 zero-free half-plane' (created and merged 8 October 2026). Claims: for every q and every a coprime to q, the least prime p(q,a) <= C(eps) q^(7/3+eps) with C effective (Theorem A), given OpenAI's Theorem 1.1 (the 7/8 zero-free half-plane) and Chen-Gupta-Li's Theorem 1.2 (zero density 7/3). Theorem A' gives 12/5 'on refereed density inputs alone' (a Montgomery-Ingham-type bound and Huxley 1975). The PR records the status as 'Candidate, pending external review' and 'ordinary written proof by the hunt, unreviewed'. The repository says 'none is formalized in Lean' for its October results.
events.delivers: Part A: a claimed admissible exponent 7/3 for all moduli, conditional on OpenAI's unrefereed 7/8 theorem and on Chen-Gupta-Li's density estimate; and a claimed 12/5 (Theorem A') from inputs the PR calls refereed. The PR does not say whether A' is conditional on anything else, and that is for the judging pass.
events.remains: Parts B, C, D; Part A below 12/5; the review of the OpenAI and Chen-Gupta-Li inputs.
events.directly_checkable: The repository offers ball-arithmetic numerical enclosures and a written argument; neither was run here.
events.doubts: (1) The main claim depends on OpenAI's unrefereed 7/8 theorem and on an arXiv density estimate. (2) The PR's 'Lead review (2026-10-08)' paragraph was written on the PR author's side, not by a listed reviewer; the PR lists 'No reviews'. (3) The repository says: 'Every conditional figure above H, including this tree's, rests on an analytic bridge that no person has reviewed.' (4) The repository says the result is not formalized in Lean. (5) A general 12/5 would beat the record 5 by a wide margin, and the 2019 prime-power result cited above already had 12/5 as its prior value for a restricted class; the PR does not discuss why the general 12/5 would follow now. (6) Wikipedia's 2.4 row credits OpenAI with a corollary, while the PR derives 12/5 without OpenAI's theorem (see disputes).
events.direction: Claimed move of L to 7/3 (conditional) and to 12/5 (Theorem A'), both below the record 5; cuts toward the conjectured small L without reaching 2.

systems.name: Claude Opus 5.5
systems.what_it_did: The PR's commit trailers name Claude Opus 5.5 as co-author and its description ends 'Generated with Claude Code'. The repository says its hunts are run largely by AI agents, and the PR says 'The authoring agent did not assign evidentiary status to its own output.'

events.what_happened: Claim circulating from 21 September 2026: a proof, credited to GPT-6 Astra and announced by the anonymous account 'Captain Sude' on X, that every even integer above 2 is a sum of two integers with odd total number of prime factors (Liouville value -1). A KuCoin flash headline calls it 'Linnik's variant of the Goldbach conjecture'. The KuCoin page gives no paper or repository link. A GitHub issue tracking provenance (ai4math-chronicle #116) exists and was not opened.
events.delivers: A Liouville-valued Goldbach-type statement. It is not Linnik's constant and not the Linnik-Goldbach problem (primes plus powers of 2). Excluded by scope; the 'Linnik' in the headline is a name collision.
events.remains: All of Parts A-E.
events.doubts: Anonymous announcer; the KuCoin page is a secondary aggregator; the claim of a Lean formalization and 'independent audits' names no auditors and gives no link.
events.direction: Not applicable to this bullet.

disputes.summary: Wikipedia's Linnik article (2026 version) lists 'L <= 2.4 (OpenAI, 2026), corollary of 7/8 Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis', added in an edit of 7 October 2026. OpenAI's manuscript states no Linnik consequence; the John D. Cook post names only the prime-number-theorem error term; and the 12/5 figure appears in teal-sea PR #277 as Theorem A', which the PR says rests on refereed inputs alone and does not use OpenAI's theorem. The 7/3 figure in the same PR does use OpenAI's theorem.

The Wikipedia article cites Heath-Brown (1992) for the conjecture p(a,d) < d^2. Search summaries credit the d^2 form to Kanold and to Schinzel-Sierpinski, and credit Heath-Brown with the conjecture p(d) << d(log d)^2.

Zhao (arXiv:2511.05631) presents 'L=5 is admissible' as an improvement from 5.2, attributed to Xylouris (2009). Other sources credit L = 5 to Xylouris (2011) and 5.18 to 2009, so whether Zhao's paper gives a new bound or re-derives an existing one is disputed.
The Palomar entry for the Naslund 3.99 paper is PALOMAR-2026-10-01-000020 in the repository's README and PALOMAR-2026-10-01-000018 in the Wikipedia citation. The registry entry page was not readable.

Johnston and Trudgian credit an unconditional K = 7 to a Maynard-Pandey-Radziwill announcement, which they call preliminary and do not list as a theorem. The arXiv text of the Maynard-Pandey-Radziwill paper mentions no announcement. A separate search snippet credits the N^(19/24) improvement to Maynard alone.

A KuCoin headline calls the Liouville-valued Goldbach claim credited to GPT-6 Astra 'Linnik's variant of the Goldbach conjecture'. The claim concerns a Liouville analogue of Goldbach and is not about Linnik's theorem or Linnik's constant.

summary: The bullet names no problem; it links 'Linnik's theorem', so the record reads it as the problems the linked article itself lists: Linnik's constant L (Part A), the bound p(a,d) < d^2 (Part B), with the article's conditional GRH bound (Part D) as context and Heath-Brown's d(log d)^2 form (Part C) from the literature. The Linnik-Goldbach problem (Part E, K powers of 2) is recorded as a second reading the article does not name. Forty-seven web searches and about forty-five page fetches found no event that settles the value of L. In-window events on Part A: Matomaki-Merikoski-Terävainen (31 January 2024; unconditional exponent 350, weaker than the record); Fiori (April 2024; numerical conjecture); Zhao (7 November 2025; claims L = 5, which is already the record, with Theorem 1.3's proof omitted in the text read); Bruna (26 March 2026; exponent 2+eps under GLH only); Kandhil-Languasco-Moree (16 July 2026; k^(1+o(1)) under GRH plus a pair-correlation hypothesis); Naslund (1-2 October 2026; claimed L <= 3.99 for sufficiently large moduli; the authors state that Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT Astra 6 wrote the paper under their prompting and supervision; the Lean files are sorry-free but the bound itself is not formalised; no human review is recorded; the Wikipedia Linnik article was edited on 7 October 2026 by the account 'Enaslund' to add the 3.99 row, which is a self-citation rather than uptake); and teal-sea PR #277 (8 October 2026; claimed L <= 7/3 conditional on OpenAI's unrefereed 7/8 zero-free region and Chen-Gupta-Li's density estimate, and 12/5 on Theorem A' which the PR calls refereed-input-only; written with Claude Opus 5.5 per its commit trailers; no reviews). OpenAI's family-003 manuscript (dated 30 September, public 6 October 2026) states no Linnik consequence and is not withdrawn; its only bearing on Part A is through the third-party derivations. The Wikipedia 2.4 row attributes 12/5 to OpenAI as a corollary, which the PR's own derivation contradicts. Part E: Johnston-Trudgian (18 May 2026) give K = 6 under GRH; the unconditional K = 7 rests on a preliminary announcement that they do not list as a theorem; Maynard-Pandey-Radziwill (14 August 2026) is the exponential-sum input. Blomer-Brumley-Radziwill's 'joint Linnik problems' and Matomaki-Terävainen's multiplicative analogue are recorded as different problems sharing the name or a close analogue. The GPT-6 Astra Liouville-Goldbach claim (21 September 2026) is recorded as out of scope; its AI attribution comes from an anonymous announcement and secondary aggregators, and no authors' account was read. Close calls: (a) whether moves of L count when the bullet names no quantity: the linked article names L, so the record treats bounds on L as in scope, per section 2.1; (b) whether the unreviewed 3.99 and 7/3 claims 'move' L: recorded as claims with their doubts, not as settled moves; (c) whether Zhao's L = 5 is new: recorded as disputed; (d) whether conditional bounds (GLH, GRH plus a pair-correlation hypothesis) count: recorded as conditional, not as moves of the unconditional record. Dating uses the first public posting (arXiv or GitHub date, or the repository release), not journal dates; OpenAI's manuscript is dated 30 September but was first public on 6 October. AI involvement: the authors of the 3.99 paper and teal-sea's PR state AI authorship with direct quotes; no human-authored paper read in the window names an AI system.
competing_reading: The strongest case for counting the 3.99 and 7/3 claims as the problem's status is that L is the quantity the linked article names, the article's own table already records 3.99 and 2.4, and both are the first claimed improvements on the record of 5 since 2011. The opposite case: the bullet names no quantity; both claims are unreviewed, one rests on an unrefereed OpenAI theorem and the other on AI-written text whose authors describe no human check; the Wikipedia row that records them was added by the 3.99 author, so the table is not independent evidence; and Zhao's 2025 'L = 5' is the same record re-attributed. On that reading the status of the problem is unchanged since 2011, and every in-window event is a conditional, unrefereed or scope-excluded result.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A human-refereed version of the Naslund 3.99 paper, or an expert written verification of its analytic inputs (the Hypotheses table) and of the case analysis not covered by Lean. (2) A Lean proof of the bound itself rather than of the formal parts. (3) An expert check of OpenAI's family-003 theorem (the 7/8 zero-free region) and of Chen-Gupta-Li's Theorem 1.2, and a human check of teal-sea Theorem A and A'. (4) The Palomar registry text for the Naslund entry (ID mismatch) and the Hexagon listing's review statement. (5) The Wikipedia Linnik article's January 2024 revision, to fix what the frozen bullet's linked article said. (6) A ruling from the judging pass on whether the bullet is about L (named in the article) or about the wider set of problems, and on whether the Linnik-Goldbach reading (Part E) is in scope.

The 'Chen-Gupta-Li single-modulus' title did not match; the paper is arXiv:2507.08296, 'Large value estimates for Dirichlet polynomials with characters and zero density of Dirichlet L-functions'.
The Chen-Gupta-Li abstract states no least-prime-in-progression consequence, correcting one search summary that said it did.
Hitting Arithmetic Progressions at the Square-Root Scale (arXiv:2606.01780) concerns a hitting-set problem, not Linnik's theorem.
The OpenAI Liouville-Goldbach 'Linnik variant' headline concerns a different statement; the anonymous announcement and the GitHub provenance issue were not traced to a primary paper.
The Sienicki human audit (arXiv:2608.14673) covers OpenAI's 1 August 2026 batch of ten results, not family 003; no audit of the 7/8 manuscript was found.
Johnston-Trudgian's Maynard-Pandey-Radziwill citation was checked against the MPR arXiv text, which mentions no earlier announcement.
